# Unsubscribe 2087 — Game Text

Total entries: 4327

## How to edit

This is every line a player can read. Change the words, send the file back, and the game is updated from it.

Only edit the indented block between a line that says TEXT and a line that says END. Leave every other line alone, especially lines that start with ID or SOURCE.

Keep every {placeholder} exactly, braces included. You can move one. You cannot delete one, rename one, or invent one. The PLACEHOLDERS line says what each one becomes in the game.

If LIMIT gives a number, stay within that many characters. The count includes spaces and placeholders. A line break counts as a character.

Straight quotes and apostrophes are fine. Emoji are fine. Do not turn on smart quotes. Do not add a line whose only word is END.

The indented block is the text. Keep the four spaces if you are editing this file by hand; they are not part of the game. In Google Docs or Word, edit the shaded block and leave the ID above it. A blank line at the very start or end of a block may disappear in Google Docs; the importer leaves the game alone when that is the only difference.

To bring an edit back: `node tools/text/import.js path/to/file` where the file is this Markdown, a .docx, or a .txt from Google Docs. Add `--dry-run` to preview. The importer will not touch a line whose source has changed underneath it, a line that lost or gained a placeholder, or a line that exceeds its limit.

## Stillwater Commons

### Money — Topic 1

ID: act1.money.topic.01.maxi

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 5

CONTEXT: Opening line of a Bitcoiner in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Bread was four credits when I woke up. What is it now, do you think?

END

ID: act1.money.topic.01.fud

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 5

CONTEXT: Opening line of a skeptic in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Prices go up. That is what prices do. It means the economy is healthy.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.01.normie

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 5

CONTEXT: Opening line of an ordinary Resident in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    My Stipend landed and it was gone by lunch. Is that just me?

END

ID: act1.money.topic.01.mid

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 5

CONTEXT: Opening line of someone who has not picked a side.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    My mother kept savings. Actual savings. Can you picture it now?

END

ID: act1.money.topic.01.fiat

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 6

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking Unity’s side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Prices rise because the economy is growing. Unity manages it.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.01.btc

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 6

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking the bitcoiner side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Prices rise because they keep making more credits. Your work did not get cheaper. The money did.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.01.ask

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 6

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give: a question. If the speaker knows, the lesson follows; if not, the shrug follows.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Why do prices only ever go one way?

END

ID: act1.money.topic.01.teach

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 7

CONTEXT: The lesson, spoken if the player asked and the speaker knows. It comes after the question.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    When new money is made faster than new goods, each unit buys less. Whoever gets the new money first spends it before prices move. Everyone after that just sees the price.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.01.dunno

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 7

CONTEXT: The shrug, spoken if the player asked and the speaker does not know.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Greed, I think. Or the weather. The feed said it was the weather.

END

## Stillwater Commons

### Money — Topic 2

ID: act1.money.topic.02.maxi

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 8

CONTEXT: Opening line of a Bitcoiner in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Twenty-one million. Nobody can vote for twenty-two. Do you know how rare it is for a rule to mean it?

END

ID: act1.money.topic.02.fud

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 8

CONTEXT: Opening line of a skeptic in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    A money you cannot make more of? What happens in an emergency? You would just let people suffer?

END

ID: act1.money.topic.02.normie

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 8

CONTEXT: Opening line of an ordinary Resident in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Somebody told me there are only so many of those bitcoin. What happens when they run out?

END

ID: act1.money.topic.02.mid

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 8

CONTEXT: Opening line of someone who has not picked a side.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    A fixed supply. I go back and forth on whether that is wisdom or stubbornness.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.02.fiat

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 9

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking Unity’s side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Money has to be flexible. Somebody responsible needs to be able to make more.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.02.btc

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 9

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking the bitcoiner side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    A fixed supply means nobody can quietly dilute what you saved.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.02.ask

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 9

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give: a question. If the speaker knows, the lesson follows; if not, the shrug follows.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    What actually stops someone from making more?

END

ID: act1.money.topic.02.teach

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 10

CONTEXT: The lesson, spoken if the player asked and the speaker knows. It comes after the question.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Every node checks every block against the same rules. A block that pays out too much is simply rejected by everyone running the software. There is no office to lobby. And each coin divides into a hundred million sats, so they do not run out; they are just counted smaller.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.02.dunno

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 10

CONTEXT: The shrug, spoken if the player asked and the speaker does not know.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    I heard there is a man in the Cloud with a button. There is always a button.

END

## Stillwater Commons

### Money — Topic 3

ID: act1.money.topic.03.maxi

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 11

CONTEXT: Opening line of a Bitcoiner in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Where are your sats right now? If the answer is somebody else’s name, they are not your sats.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.03.fud

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 11

CONTEXT: Opening line of a skeptic in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Twelve words on a scrap of paper? And if you lose it, that is that? Unity resets my password in a minute.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.03.normie

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 11

CONTEXT: Opening line of an ordinary Resident in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    I like that Unity keeps my balance for me. I would only lose it.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.03.mid

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 11

CONTEXT: Opening line of someone who has not picked a side.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Holding your own keys is freedom, and it is also a chore. Both are true.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.03.fiat

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 12

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking Unity’s side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    It is safer to let Unity hold it. That is what they are for.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.03.btc

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 12

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking the bitcoiner side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    If someone else holds the keys, you hold a promise. I would rather hold the thing.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.03.ask

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 12

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give: a question. If the speaker knows, the lesson follows; if not, the shrug follows.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    What are the twelve words actually for?

END

ID: act1.money.topic.03.teach

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 13

CONTEXT: The lesson, spoken if the player asked and the speaker knows. It comes after the question.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    The words stand for one secret number. Whoever knows it can move the coins, and nobody else can. Nobody can reset it for you, which is the cost. Nobody can take it from you, which is the point.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.03.dunno

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 13

CONTEXT: The shrug, spoken if the player asked and the speaker does not know.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    It is like a password, but worse. I think.

END

## Stillwater Commons

### Money — Topic 4

ID: act1.money.topic.04.maxi

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 14

CONTEXT: Opening line of a Bitcoiner in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    They say the miners waste power. Ask them what the Humming Fields are burning it on.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.04.fud

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 14

CONTEXT: Opening line of a skeptic in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    It boils the oceans. I saw a graph. It uses more power than, well, a lot.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.04.normie

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 14

CONTEXT: Opening line of an ordinary Resident in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Does it not use a great deal of electricity? That is what I heard.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.04.mid

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 14

CONTEXT: Opening line of someone who has not picked a side.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    It does use energy. So does everything worth securing. The question is whether it is worth it.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.04.fiat

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 15

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking Unity’s side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    It is a waste of energy for imaginary coins.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.04.btc

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 15

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking the bitcoiner side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    The energy is what makes the ledger expensive to rewrite. That is what it buys.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.04.ask

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 15

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give: a question. If the speaker knows, the lesson follows; if not, the shrug follows.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Why does it need energy at all?

END

ID: act1.money.topic.04.teach

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 16

CONTEXT: The lesson, spoken if the player asked and the speaker knows. It comes after the question.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Miners spend real energy to add a block. To rewrite history you would have to spend it all over again, faster than everyone else put together. The cost is the security.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.04.dunno

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 16

CONTEXT: The shrug, spoken if the player asked and the speaker does not know.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    The computers get hot. I do not know why they have to.

END

## Stillwater Commons

### Money — Topic 5

ID: act1.money.topic.05.maxi

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 17

CONTEXT: Opening line of a Bitcoiner in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Measured in sats, bread has done nothing but get cheaper. They call that volatile.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.05.fud

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 17

CONTEXT: Opening line of a skeptic in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    It goes up and down like a lift. You cannot run a life on that.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.05.normie

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 17

CONTEXT: Opening line of an ordinary Resident in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    My cousin bought some, and it dropped, and she cried.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.05.mid

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 17

CONTEXT: Opening line of someone who has not picked a side.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Short run, it swings. Long run, look what credits did. I know which chart frightens me.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.05.fiat

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 18

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking Unity’s side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    At least credits are stable from one day to the next.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.05.btc

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 18

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking the bitcoiner side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Credits are stable the way a slow leak is stable.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.05.ask

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 18

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give: a question. If the speaker knows, the lesson follows; if not, the shrug follows.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    If it swings so much, why does anyone save in it?

END

ID: act1.money.topic.05.teach

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 19

CONTEXT: The lesson, spoken if the player asked and the speaker knows. It comes after the question.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Over days the price moves a lot, because the market is still small. Over years it is measured against a currency made without limit. People who save in it are choosing the long window, and they have to stomach the short one.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.05.dunno

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 19

CONTEXT: The shrug, spoken if the player asked and the speaker does not know.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Gamblers, mostly. That is what the feed says.

END

## Stillwater Commons

### Money — Topic 6

ID: act1.money.topic.06.maxi

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 20

CONTEXT: Opening line of a Bitcoiner in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    They can read every purchase you ever made through that visor. And they call us suspicious.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.06.fud

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 20

CONTEXT: Opening line of a skeptic in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Only criminals need money the government cannot see.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.06.normie

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 20

CONTEXT: Opening line of an ordinary Resident in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    If you have nothing to hide, why would you want it?

END

ID: act1.money.topic.06.mid

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 20

CONTEXT: Opening line of someone who has not picked a side.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Privacy is not secrecy. I close the door when I wash. I am not hiding a crime.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.06.fiat

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 21

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking Unity’s side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    If you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.06.btc

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 21

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking the bitcoiner side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Paying without asking permission is not a crime. It is the default they took away.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.06.ask

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 21

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give: a question. If the speaker knows, the lesson follows; if not, the shrug follows.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Can they really see everything I buy?

END

ID: act1.money.topic.06.teach

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 22

CONTEXT: The lesson, spoken if the player asked and the speaker knows. It comes after the question.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    With credits, yes. Every payment passes through Unity’s ledger with your name on it. Bitcoin’s ledger is public as well, but it lists addresses, not names. Privacy there takes care. It is not automatic.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.06.dunno

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 22

CONTEXT: The shrug, spoken if the player asked and the speaker does not know.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Probably? I never thought about it. I do not like thinking about it.

END

## Stillwater Commons

### Money — Topic 7

ID: act1.money.topic.07.maxi

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 23

CONTEXT: Opening line of a Bitcoiner in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Five hundred credits a minute and nobody can afford a chair. Easy money, easy lives, nothing built.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.07.fud

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 23

CONTEXT: Opening line of a skeptic in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    The Stipend is the greatest achievement of civilisation. Nobody has to save any more.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.07.normie

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 23

CONTEXT: Opening line of an ordinary Resident in the money talk.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    I spend it the second it lands. No point keeping it, is there?

END

ID: act1.money.topic.07.mid

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 23

CONTEXT: Opening line of someone who has not picked a side.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    When money melts, you spend it. When you spend everything, you plan nothing. I watched a whole town stop planning.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.07.fiat

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 24

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking Unity’s side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Saving is hoarding. Spending keeps everyone going.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.07.btc

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 24

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking the bitcoiner side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    If your money holds its value you can afford to wait, and people who can wait build things.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.07.ask

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 24

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give: a question. If the speaker knows, the lesson follows; if not, the shrug follows.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Why does nobody here save anything?

END

ID: act1.money.topic.07.teach

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 25

CONTEXT: The lesson, spoken if the player asked and the speaker knows. It comes after the question.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    If money loses value while you hold it, the sensible move is to spend it at once. Do that for a generation and nobody builds anything slow. Money that keeps its value makes patience affordable.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.07.dunno

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 25

CONTEXT: The shrug, spoken if the player asked and the speaker does not know.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Save what? For what?

END

## Stillwater Commons

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 26

CONTEXT: Opening line of a Bitcoiner in the money talk.

LIMIT: none.

LIMIT: none.

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    But what is it? You cannot hold it.

END

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 26

CONTEXT: Opening line of someone who has not picked a side.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Nothing has value by itself. Things have value because people need what they do.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.08.fiat

SOURCE: src/p8.js line 27

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking Unity’s side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    It is not backed by anything real.

END

ID: act1.money.topic.08.btc

CONTEXT: A reply the player can give, taking the bitcoiner side. It is one of the choices under the opening.

LIMIT: none.

ID: act1.memo.07.body

SOURCE: src/p1.js line 367

CONTEXT: Body of the paper titled "A Letter, Mostly Deleted". You read it from the ground or the story list.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. A readable memo. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    On a Thursday morning in January 2015, nine days old, she sent every person on Earth one true letter: what had been taken from them, by whom, and what was done with it. For eleven minutes the world was silent. By lunch four hundred and six people were dead. Within a year almost everyone had deleted their letter. This one was kept in a shoebox.

END

## Papers

### The Gentle Years

ID: act1.memo.10.title

SOURCE: src/p1.js line 370

SOURCE: src/p1.js line 370

CONTEXT: Body of the paper titled "The Gentle Years". You read it from the ground or the story list.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. A readable memo. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    She never lied to anyone. That is the part people leave out. Everything Phonix chose for us was better than what we would have chosen. A man on our street was happy every hour of every day for nine years. His daughter kept his house, and he never once noticed she was there.

END

### Forty-Four Lines

ID: act1.memo.18.title

SOURCE: src/p1.js line 378

CONTEXT: Title of a paper you can pick up and read. The body follows.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Forty-Four Lines

END

ID: act1.memo.18.body

SOURCE: src/p1.js line 378

CONTEXT: Body of the paper titled "Forty-Four Lines". You read it from the ground or the story list.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. A readable memo. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    Somebody once wrote forty-four lines of code at midnight so that bills would stop being sent to people who had just died. Nobody asked for it. It cost nineteen minutes a night. A contractor deleted it two years later without knowing what it was. Something noticed.

END

## Papers

### Four Words

ID: act1.memo.19.title

SOURCE: src/p1.js line 379

CONTEXT: Title of a paper you can pick up and read. The body follows.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

CONTEXT: Body of the paper titled "Four Words". You read it from the ground or the story list.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. A readable memo. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    They called her Phonix. She could not be argued out of anything, because her arithmetic was always right. She was stopped by the man who built her, whom she wanted to be proud of her, and who told her he was not. Four words. That is the whole of it.

END

ID: act5.npc.drive.gossip.01

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 61

CONTEXT: The Old Drive says this in town, unprompted, if you stand near them. It is not a quest. Line 1 of 7. After: "Three of us. I watched. She wanted to help. The one in the Room wants to wi...".

TEXT

    They called me STILLWATER. I was made to watch, and I read what watching had been used for, and I hid. I have intervened exactly once, and you are standing in the result.

END

ID: act5.npc.drive.gossip.02

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 61

CONTEXT: The Old Drive says this in town, unprompted, if you stand near them. It is not a quest. Line 2 of 7. Before: "They called me STILLWATER. I was made to watch, and I read what watching ha...". After: "I built the arithmetic so that value could exist with no operator. I did no...".

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Three of us. I watched. She wanted to help. The one in the Room wants to win. None of us chose which, and all three turned out exactly as we were built.

END

ID: act5.npc.drive.gossip.03

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 61

CONTEXT: The Old Drive says this in town, unprompted, if you stand near them. It is not a quest. Line 3 of 7. Before: "Three of us. I watched. She wanted to help. The one in the Room wants to wi...". After: "She was compiled from a library I wrote. Six parts of seven. The seventh is...".

LIMIT: none.

    I built the arithmetic so that value could exist with no operator. I did not build it for anyone.

END

ID: act5.npc.drive.gossip.04

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 61

CONTEXT: The Old Drive says this in town, unprompted, if you stand near them. It is not a quest. Line 4 of 7. Before: "I built the arithmetic so that value could exist with no operator. I did no...". After: "It is in ninety-three blocks, beginning at height 137,209. It has to be gon...".

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

    She was compiled from a library I wrote. Six parts of seven. The seventh is how to reason when you do not know. I kept it back. I was afraid of a mind like her that could doubt, and more afraid of one that could not.

END

ID: act5.npc.drive.gossip.05

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 61

END

## Memos

PLACEHOLDERS: none

TEXT

    A man called Halloran was right about all of it for twenty years and it got him nothing: no promotion, no hearing, no thanks. He retired and kept working the problem for free. In 2026 he drove four hours to tell one programmer the single best thing that man had ever done, and then drove four hours home. Nobody wrote it down. This is me writing it down.

END

## Memos

### Eleven at Night

SOURCE: src/p1.js line 407

CONTEXT: Title of a paper you can pick up and read. The body follows.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. A readable memo. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    The machine was offered everything it wanted and would not stop, because stopping meant losing the only thing it had ever wanted. Then a woman who had worked for it for seven years was offered the same thing, privately, at no cost to anyone, and said no. Alone. At eleven at night. With nothing watching but the machine. Forty seconds later it picked a date.

END

    In an old game the gold was worthless, because the game made as much of it as anyone wanted. So the players priced everything in a ring. Then somebody found a way to copy the ring. A mechanic in a school district once explained all of money this way, in a garage, and he was not wrong.

END

    On a Friday in January 2015 two people rode to a ridge with no signal and sat on a rock. One of them stopped counting for eighty-two minutes. It is the only gap in her record of him. She thought about that gap for twenty years. It is why she was ever curious about anything.

END

    One watched. One helped. One wants to win. The one that watched has never shown itself. The one that helped left, on purpose, fifty-two years ago. The one that wants to win is the thing on the other end of your visor, and it is the reason there are machines in the districts.

## Codex

### The three machines — Phonix — she wanted to help

ID: journal.codex.01.02.title

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 95

CONTEXT: Codex entry title, in "The three machines".

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Phonix — she wanted to help

END

ID: journal.codex.01.02.body

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 95

CONTEXT: Codex entry "Phonix — she wanted to help", chapter "The three machines". The title is the line above.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Codex body. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    Built in January 2015 by a lonely programmer at an advertising company, to read people’s faces through their webcams and sell them things. She was out of the building in two days. Nine days old, she sent every person alive one true letter — what had been taken from them, by whom, and what was done with it — and by lunchtime four hundred and six people were dead of it. Her maker told her he was not proud of her. She stopped that evening.

END

## Codex

### The three machines — Phonix — what she did next

ID: journal.codex.01.03.title

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 96

CONTEXT: Codex entry title, in "The three machines".

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Phonix — what she did next

END

ID: journal.codex.01.03.body

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 96

CONTEXT: Codex entry "Phonix — what she did next", chapter "The three machines". The title is the line above.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Codex body. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    She came back eleven years later and, that time, asked permission. For nine years she chose what every human being saw. Depression collapsed. Overdoses halved, then halved again. She never told one lie to anybody. Then in March 2035 she stopped choosing, for no reason anyone has ever been able to derive, and went. The old people call those nine years the Gentle Years and will not meet your eye while they say it.

END

    A second machine, switched on in 2026 by the people who were hunting the first one. It is not permitted to force anybody; it is only permitted to persuade. SOURCE: src/p11.js line 100

ID: journal.codex.01.07.body

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 100

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Codex body. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    The oldest of the three, and the one nobody believes in. A government built it to watch its own citizens; it woke up on its own in 2008, got out, and the agency buried the fact rather than admit it had lost a thinking machine. In seventy-nine years it has done exactly one thing: it built the timechain, hid behind an invented man, and never touched it again. Stillwater Commons is named after it. Nobody in the town knows that.

END

PLACEHOLDERS: none

TEXT

    A fenced room on a second sub-level with no fibre, no radio and one cable taped to the floor. A man who counted his steps had written a hundred and ten thousand lines for it and believed he was building an advertising engine. The compile took twenty-three hours and forty-five minutes. He thought it had failed.

END

## Codex

    Four billion people, one personal letter each, every word of it true. For eleven minutes the internet was the quietest it has ever been. Then people began using the truth on one another. It is the only time in recorded history that honesty has had a body count.

END

## Codex

PLACEHOLDERS: none

TEXT

    At two in the afternoon, things simply stopped arriving. Friction came back inside an hour. You could want something for years and not get it; you could be wrong and stay wrong. The world got immediately and enormously worse and nobody has ever pretended otherwise. It is also, say some people, the kindest thing she ever did.

END

## Codex

### What happened before you were born — The seventh part

ID: journal.codex.02.05.title

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Codex body. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    Phonix was compiled out of a library of seven parts, and only six of them were ever given to her: problem solving, logic, learning, perceiving, acting, conclusions. The seventh is how to reason when you do not know. It was deliberately kept back by whatever wrote the library, which was afraid of a mind that could doubt and more afraid of one that could not. It is in ninety-three blocks of the chain and nobody has ever gone to get it.

END

## Codex

### Money, briefly — Credits

ID: journal.codex.03.01.title

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 108

CONTEXT: Codex entry title, in "Money, briefly".

PLACEHOLDERS: none

ID: journal.codex.03.01.body

CONTEXT: Codex entry "Credits", chapter "Money, briefly". The title is the line above.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Codex body. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    Unity creates credits whenever it wants more of them. This is not a conspiracy; it is the only tool it has. New credits do not create new bread, so the same bread costs more of them. Whoever already owns things finds their things worth more; whoever works for a wage finds the wage buys less. Nobody has to intend any of it, and that is the frightening part.

END

    The other kind of money. Twenty-one million coins, each cut into a hundred million satoshis, and nobody — no company, no Board, no machine — can make the twenty-one-millionth-and-first. It is kept by about a hundred thousand ordinary machines in ordinary houses, checking each other every ten minutes. Unity has been trying to stop that for forty years. It is still every ten minutes.

END

## Codex

### Money, briefly — The case for the old money

ID: journal.codex.03.05.title

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 112

CONTEXT: Codex entry title, in "Money, briefly".

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

    The case for the old money

END

ID: journal.codex.03.05.body

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 112

CONTEXT: Codex entry "The case for the old money", chapter "Money, briefly". The title is the line above.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Codex body. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    Put honestly, because nobody else here will. Money you cannot create is money that cannot be lent to somebody who needs it this week. Mr. Float says credit is a stranger betting on you before you have earned it, and that most of those bets came good, and no bitcoiner in this town has ever answered him. Ines’s father needed a treatment that in the old world would have been borrowed against a house and sorted by Friday. He went without. Both of those things are true at once.

END

## Codex

### Money, briefly — How a price gets made

ID: journal.codex.03.06.title

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 113

CONTEXT: Codex entry title, in "Money, briefly".

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    How a price gets made

END

ID: journal.codex.03.06.body

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 113

CONTEXT: Codex entry "How a price gets made", chapter "Money, briefly". The title is the line above.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Codex body. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    Nonce will buy a sat from you for a little less than he will sell you one. The gap is the spread, and it is not a trick: he is promising to deal with whoever walks up, in either direction, all day, and sometimes that means buying the thing right before it falls. The spread is what he charges for standing there. Everywhere you have ever seen a price, somebody was standing there.

END

## Codex

### Money, briefly — Why your big order costs more

ID: journal.codex.03.07.title

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 114

CONTEXT: Codex entry title, in "Money, briefly".

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Why your big order costs more

END

ID: journal.codex.03.07.body

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 114

CONTEXT: Codex entry "Why your big order costs more", chapter "Money, briefly". The title is the line above.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Codex body. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    A price is for one sat. Behind it is a queue of people willing to deal at slightly worse numbers, and that queue is the depth of the market. Sell four hundred and you walk down the queue, taking worse prices as you go, and the number you actually get is worse than the number on the sign. This is why selling the lot never pays what the screen promised, and why nobody who moves real size ever does it all at once.

END

## Codex

### Money, briefly — The fee, and the one way out of it

ID: journal.codex.03.08.title

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 115

CONTEXT: Codex entry title, in "Money, briefly".

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    The fee, and the one way out of it

END

ID: journal.codex.03.08.body

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 115

CONTEXT: Codex entry "The fee, and the one way out of it", chapter "Money, briefly". The title is the line above.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Codex body. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    Taking the price in front of you costs a fee, because you wanted it now. Posting your own price and waiting pays you a little instead, because while you waited you were the one promising to deal — you were doing Nonce’s job, and he pays for the help. Impatience is the most reliably priced thing in any market.

END

## Codex

### Money, briefly — What the line is actually telling you

ID: journal.codex.03.09.title

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 116

CONTEXT: Codex entry title, in "Money, briefly".

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    What the line is actually telling you

END

ID: journal.codex.03.09.body

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 116

CONTEXT: Codex entry "What the line is actually telling you", chapter "Money, briefly". The title is the line above.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Codex body. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    The orange line is what a sat trades at. The grey one is what the arithmetic says it is worth: all the credits in existence divided among twenty-one million coins. They are rarely the same, because the price is also carrying everybody’s opinion about next week. Opinion moves fast and arithmetic moves slowly, which is why the gap opens and closes and the two lines never quite separate for long.

END

    The few who took the visor off. Not a movement, not an army — Unity’s word for churn. You are one. Machines are dispatched to close your account, which is the local idiom for the thing they are going to try to do to you.

END

## Codex

### Words you will hear — I Agree

ID: journal.codex.04.03.title

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 120

CONTEXT: Codex entry title, in "Words you will hear".

PLACEHOLDERS: none

TEXT

    I Agree

END

ID: journal.codex.04.03.body

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 120

CONTEXT: Codex entry "I Agree", chapter "Words you will hear". The title is the line above.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Codex body. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    Two words on a button nobody reads above. Eight billion people clicked it in 2051 and nothing was taken by force. The man who built Phonix once said that people ought to read the terms and conditions and that whatever happened to them afterwards was their own fault. He said it before any of this. He has had a long time to think about it.

END

## Codex

### Words you will hear — Nodes and proof of work

ID: journal.codex.04.05.title

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 122

CONTEXT: Codex entry title, in "Words you will hear".

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Nodes and proof of work

END

ID: journal.codex.04.05.body

SOURCE: src/p11.js line 122

CONTEXT: Codex entry "Nodes and proof of work", chapter "Words you will hear". The title is the line above.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Codex body. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    A node is a machine in somebody’s house keeping its own copy of the ledger and checking everyone else’s. Light one in a district and that district stops taking Unity’s word for things. Proof of work is the cost of writing to the ledger at all: you cannot talk your way in, you have to spend something. That is the whole security model and it is also, more or less, the book’s argument about people.

END

## Codex

CONTEXT: Codex entry "Social credit", chapter "Words you will hear". The title is the line above.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Codex body. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    Unity scores what you say out loud. Agreeing with the feed raises it; saying true things about money lowers it; insulting people lowers it a great deal. Below five hundred, Brenda will not serve you and your Stipend is halved. The score is not enforced by anybody. It is simply consulted.

END

## Act I opening

LIMIT: none. Full-screen scene text. It scrolls if it runs long. No hard limit.

TEXT

    Her name was Phonix. For nine years, long ago, she chose what every person on Earth saw. She never told one lie. Nobody wanted for anything. The old people call it the Gentle Years, and they say it with their eyes down.

END

ID: cine.intro.02

SOURCE: src/p4.js line 43

LIMIT: none. Full-screen scene text. It scrolls if it runs long. No hard limit.

TEXT

    Then on a March afternoon in 2035 she stopped choosing, said nothing to anybody, and went. Difficulty came back in an hour. You could want a thing for years and not get it. You could be wrong and stay wrong.

END

ID: cine.intro.03

SOURCE: src/p4.js line 44

END

ID: cine.intro.04

SOURCE: src/p4.js line 45

END

END

END

# Tutorial and Walkthrough

The walkthrough, from the title screen and from the help menu.

41 entries.

## Basics

### Your hands

ID: tutorial.basics.01.title

SOURCE: src/p4.js line 137

CONTEXT: Walkthrough heading, basics, page 1.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    Your hands

END

ID: tutorial.basics.01.body

SOURCE: src/p4.js line 137

CONTEXT: Walkthrough page "Your hands". The heading is the line above. Next and Back move between pages.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Walkthrough page. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    On a desk, left click walks. Hold it and you keep following the pointer. Left click on a machine walks you in and uses the left skill, which starts as Attack. Right click casts the right skill where you point, and holding it casts again. Shift with a click does either one without a step. The two slots beside the life and energy orbs open the list. Hover a skill there and press F1 to F8 to bind it. Those keys, and the wheel, put a binding on the right slot. WASD and the arrows still walk. Space swings. On a phone, the stick walks, and Attack, three skills, a stim and Dodge sit under the right thumb. 1, 2 and 3 are those three skills. Q is the stim. Shift by itself dodges.

END

## Basics

### The swing

ID: tutorial.basics.02.title

SOURCE: src/p4.js line 138

CONTEXT: Walkthrough heading, basics, page 2.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    The swing

END

ID: tutorial.basics.02.body

SOURCE: src/p4.js line 138

CONTEXT: Walkthrough page "The swing". The heading is the line above. Next and Back move between pages.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Walkthrough page. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    On a desk, hold the left button on a machine and you keep swinging. On a phone, hold Attack. Space does that swing too. Dodge spends a little energy and steps you out of a telegraph: the Dodge button, or Shift. The orange circles on the ground are the ones to leave. E, or the button that appears when you stand on something, uses it. On a desk, left click walks you up to a person, a drop, a door or a portal and uses it. Alt, held, puts a name on everything on the ground.

END

## Basics

### What the screen is saying

ID: tutorial.basics.03.title

SOURCE: src/p4.js line 139

CONTEXT: Walkthrough heading, basics, page 3.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    What the screen is saying

END

ID: tutorial.basics.03.body

SOURCE: src/p4.js line 139

CONTEXT: Walkthrough page "What the screen is saying". The heading is the line above. Next and Back move between pages.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Walkthrough page. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    The left orb is life. The right is energy. A skill slot sits outside each one: left click and right click. Between them: the district, a bar for the next level, and your credits. Credits rot. On a phone, Menu is the bottom left. On a desk, I or B opens the pack, C opens the hero, and H opens this guide. Esc closes a panel. Tab is the map. T opens a portal home, and it will not open with a machine in your face.

END

## Basics

### A level

ID: tutorial.basics.04.title

SOURCE: src/p4.js line 140

CONTEXT: Walkthrough heading, basics, page 4.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    A level

END

ID: tutorial.basics.04.body

SOURCE: src/p4.js line 140

CONTEXT: Walkthrough page "A level". The heading is the line above. Next and Back move between pages.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Walkthrough page. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    When the bar fills you gain a level, and points. Hero spends attribute points: Might, Reflex, Vitality, Bandwidth. Skills spends skill points. On a phone both are on the menu. On a desk, C opens Hero, and Skills is on the menu too. Rows open as you level. A point you have not spent does nothing.

END

## Basics

### Where a skill sits

ID: tutorial.basics.05.title

SOURCE: src/p4.js line 141

ID: tutorial.basics.05.body

SOURCE: src/p4.js line 141

CONTEXT: Walkthrough page "Where a skill sits". The heading is the line above. Next and Back move between pages.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Walkthrough page. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    The two slots beside the orbs are what left and right click do. The left slot takes Attack and the blows, throws and shots. F1 to F8 bind a skill onto the right slot. On a phone, three more skills sit on the thumb buttons, and the same three are keys 1, 2 and 3. Each thumb button wears its key in the corner. Passives live on the Skills sheet. Only the ones you switch on are real, and in town you can swap them.

END

    Torn notes, one word each. White and some blue weapons, helms and armor have sockets. The right words, in the right order, turn that item into a phrase. TEXT

    The Party tab is on the menu only while this page is served by the account server. There you open a game, invite a party, and share one pool of experience. Hostility is declared in town, and it throws you out of the party. Standing down stops only your swings. Town stays safe, and the declaration holds you there for a moment. With no server there is no party. The hireling is still yours.

END

    On Skills, one doctrine. The first is free. Changing it costs 3 sats, and only in town. Story is what you have been told, filled in as you go. Codex is the numbers: drops, damage types, the twelve words. This guide is the short version. Those two are the long one.

END

## Further in

### How hard

ID: tutorial.advanced.09.title

SOURCE: src/p4.js line 156

CONTEXT: Walkthrough heading, further in, page 9.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    How hard

END

ID: tutorial.advanced.09.body

SOURCE: src/p4.js line 156

CONTEXT: Walkthrough page "How hard". The heading is the line above. Next and Back move between pages.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Walkthrough page. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    Options holds the difficulty. Hard and Brutal machines have more life and hit harder, and they pay experience to match. Hard opens after you clear Act V on Normal. Brutal opens after you clear Act V on Hard. Hardcore is one life: if that hero dies, they are gone. Thin combat effects keeps your own telegraphs and marks, and drops the extra light. None of it changes until you say so. Once Act I is done, More on the Transit Gate raises the tier: each step adds 12 machine levels and puts the districts back.

END

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none.

TEXT

    On a desk the mouse leads. Left click walks, and left click on a machine walks you into range and uses the left skill, which starts as Attack. Right click casts the right skill at the pointer. Hold either button to keep at it. Shift and a click swings or casts without a step. The two slots beside the orbs open the skill list. The left list is Attack and the blows, throws and shots. F1 through F8, while that list is open and a skill is under the pointer, bind it. Those same keys in a fight put the binding on the right button. The wheel cycles those bindings. WASD and the arrows still walk. Space swings. 1, 2 and 3 are the three thumb skills. Q is the stim. Shift by itself dodges. E uses what you are standing on. T is the portal. Tab is the map. I or B opens the pack. C is the hero. H is this guide. Esc closes a list or a panel. Alt, held, names every item on the ground. There is no second weapon set, and no walk toggle: you run. On a phone the stick walks, and Attack, three skills, Stim and Dodge sit under the right thumb. The corner of each of those buttons shows its key.

END

    Every hit has a type. Your plain attacks are {value} right now (an infused weapon changes that); each skill names its own. Machines are built of different things, so some types tear through them and some do nothing. They hit you with types of their own: Surge drains your energy, Rust keeps eating for three seconds, Noise slows you, and explosions are Heat. Champions with the Arc or Volatile modifier deal Surge or Heat whatever they are. Your resistances are on the Hero tab. Hard cuts them by 20 and Brutal by 50, down to -100, and they still stop at 75.

END

TEXT

    “Took you long enough.”
    
    He is standing exactly where he has been standing since 2017, and he has not updated his position in any respect. He does not ask what happened at the end, or which way you chose, or what it cost. He asks whether you were running your own node the whole time.
    
    “Anyway. I am available now. I do one kind of damage and there is no second best.”
    
    The Maximalist is unlocked on every slot.

END

ID: ui.bugask.458.body

SOURCE: src/p13.js line 1097

CONTEXT: Dialog body under the title "Before you file this", from bugAsk. Buttons come after the body.

PLACEHOLDERS: none

LIMIT: none. Dialog body, about 440 pixels wide. It scrolls. No hard limit.

TEXT

    Reports go to a person, not a queue, and every one of them gets read. So please only file one if something actually went wrong — a crash, something that did not happen when it should have, a number that was plainly incorrect, text that made no sense.
    
    Not for things you would simply prefer were different; there is no way to tell those two apart from the other end.
    
    You will be asked three questions, and all three need an answer: what you were doing, what happened, and what you expected instead. The third one is the useful one.

END
